utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I would like you to stay just a couple of minutes but in the other seat, it's okay. I have a question for you later on. But the setting up the proceed -- and the [indiscernible] can start now. I'll start with it right now. Last week, Friday, I asked Ms. Edgerton whether document Exhibit P3276 concerned scheduled indictment A 11 which was removed from the indictment. Ms. Edgerton responded that scheduled incident A 11 was duplicative of scheduled incident B 16.2, which remains in the indictment. I have noted that incidents A 11 refers to less victims than incident B 16.2 and covers a broader time-period. Further, the two incidents are worded in a way whereby it is now readily apparent that they are duplicative. So having said that, I wonder whether you could explain how these two incidents are duplicative and whether the Chamber and the accused were notified of this. I will leave it either to you, Mr. Tieger or Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for one moment, then, Your Honours, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think I can answer now, Your Honours. The notification that Your Honours referred to is at page 17954, which is the Registry court page number, of confidential appendix B to the pre-trial brief that we filed in -- or on 19 May 2009 in respect of the dropped scheduled incident A 11.1 as follows. This incident (11.1) refers to the same incident as schedule B 16.2. Schedule B 16.2 is to be retained. So the notice was drawn in our pre-trial brief on 19 May 2009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll take a look at that. Thank you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And before we begin to hear the cross-examination of the next or the previous witness, there are a certain number of administrative matters. First thing is a question for Mr. Robinson or Mr. Karadzic. You will have noticed the Chamber legal staff has been receiving proofing notes of Prosecution witnesses at the same time you received them recently. The legal staff then will forward these notes to the Judges of the Chamber. Do you have any objection to this practice?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And could I -- inform us where we are in terms of the testimony of Mr. Diego Arria. My information is that you told the Chamber that there had been some developments in relation to that and are seeking some guidance from the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. In the most recent, unofficial working witness list of remaining witnesses that the Prosecution provided to us without being -- that being any binding obligation upon them, they had indicated that Ambassador Aria was no longer on their active witness list, which prompted me to ask them whether or not it would be advisable for us to withdraw our application for a binding order to Venezuela and the United Nations, given that the Venezuelans and the people in the UN are doing a lot of work to collect documents that are relevant only because Ambassador Arria is a witness. And in the end of our -- some correspondence that we had, they basically said that they were not in a position to guarantee that he was not going to testify and it was up to us whether we wanted to withdraw the motion or not, which prompted me to ask the Chamber or inquire of the Chamber whether or not, should we withdraw the motion, we would be given enough time in the event that Ambassador Aria were later to be decided to be put back on the active witness list, to obtain those documents before we would be required to cross-examine him. If we had that assurance, we'd be prepared to withdraw the motion. If we don't have that assurance, then we feel that the machinations need to go forward, because if he's called as a witness, we want to have that material. So that was my inquiry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With respect to that binding order itself, speaking for myself, it is entirely up to you and Mr. Karadzic whether or not to withdraw them. However, given that both Venezuela and the United Nations are actively co-operating with you in this matter and that a lot of work has been done already, it may be wise to allow them to complete the process of review and delivery of documents, in the event that Prosecution eventually changes its mind and moves Mr. Arria back to the list of active witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But given this development, Mr. Robinson, I wonder whether there's still a need for the Chamber to impose a dead-line on Venezuela and the United Nations for the production of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think that's entirely up to you, Mr. President. We just want to be in a position to have those documents by the time and if Ambassador Arria testifies. So if you feel that no dead-line is necessary, then that's fine. In my own -- in the ordinary way of doing things, I would think that these people need dead-lines because they haven't obeyed the ones that -- the working dates that we've had in the past have slipped. So I would prefer that they be given dead-lines so that our expectations are on the same wavelength, but it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In light of the reasons I referred to, the Chamber will dismiss your request to impose dead-lines on Venezuela and the United Nations, which was filed on 15th of August. The Chamber would also encourage the Prosecution to inform everybody, if that happens - that means the -- Mr. Arria being back to the list of active witnesses - as soon as it happens so that the accused and the Chamber can prepare for that witness in a timely manner. One ancillary matter, Mr. Robinson. I think that both Venezuela and the United Nations should be provided with a transcript of this discussion so that they are on notice that there will be no dead-line and that Mr. Diego Arria may not be called to give evidence in this case after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. President. And if you like, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And if you could update the Chamber as to where we are in terms of the ICMP -- the request for -- request to ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think we've made a lot of progress with ICMP. The latest communication which we received last week is that they are compiling the list of names and are going to forward them to us. Once they've done that, and they've also forward the DNA and bone profiles of victims that they would need to provide, Dr. Karadzic will select five names from the list and we will begin the process of the first stage of sampling ICMP documents, which is to give five known names and test those. After that, this process is complete, we will begin the random sampling of 295 samples, for which we've agreed that the Prosecution's expert Dr. Parsons and our expert Dr. Stojkovic will consult and come up with the method of random sampling. But it seems like we're on a path to an agreement with the ICMP as to how to proceed, and the previous issues that had blocked our progress seem to have now been resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I still note that the Prosecution's request for further orders in relation to ICMP is still pending before the Chamber. I wonder whether, given the recent development, the Prosecution's request should be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm -- I can't claim a sufficiently nuanced grasp of the details of the discussions to take a declarative position at this point. I will say, however, that my understanding has been that what has been cast as supposed progress is not the case at all. That the ICMP position has been clear and consistent throughout. That the accused has persistently interposed new conditions which are in conflict with the Court's order. And that the representations made today about some kind of agreement or new circumstances do not accurately reflect the situation. And I would certainly be loathed to suggest any kind of withdrawal of the motion without further clarification with those who have been dealing directly with this issue. I think that the Trial Chamber's previous order has to be complied with in a manner it has not been and that has been made clear in the previous pleadings and submissions. But I will double-check on the nature of these representations and get back to the Court forthwith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. There's another minor matter in relation to a Prosecution motion for leave to add one document in relation to KDZ-464. I take it he is not protected -- not a protected witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the individual I addressed Your Honours on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- in private session, these matters having arisen only yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no opposition to that addition of one document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's granted. Thank you. Unless there are any other matters, we'll bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is one other matter, and that deals with the witness who's going to come after this, because we received a proofing note for that witness, which I assume the Chamber has also received, and which makes a number of corrections to his statement. And again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I haven't -- we haven't looked at -- until we get a clearance from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, when you look at it, you'll see there's about two pages of corrections to his statement, and Dr. Karadzic just received that this morning at 11.00. Obviously he hasn't had a chance to look at it and won't have a chance to look at it. So we would ask that -- I don't know what the timing would be, but that his cross-examination would be -- it would be preferable if it can start tomorrow, because we simply didn't have -- Dr. Karadzic simply hasn't had any time at all to review that new material. Secondly, with respect to this witness, we're wondering whether or not he has testified before in the court in Bosnia, because the Prosecution had made an undertaking to notify us as part of their proofing whenever a witness had given testimony in a prior case. We've gotten no notification about this witness, but we seem to have some information that he has testified before. And we would like to be informed of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor, do you have the answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I have the answer on both parts, both points. First of all, the proofing note is one page in length. It covers typographical errors which are really very detailed. The witness is a police officer with an admirable sense of attention to the detail of his statement, so I took down every single typographical correction he wished to make, and there's nothing of substance whatsoever in the proofing note which would justify postponement of cross-examination. The second point is that the witness has testified previously at the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina and we have disclosed to the Defence his testimony in that trial. That was done several weeks ago, and I can find the precise date if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. President, we would prefer the date -- we'd like to know the date of that disclosure because we didn't find it in our disclosure lot. I just looked before even standing up and asking that, and I didn't find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Reid is working very hard on that, and you will have the answer. We can bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hurko. Please make yourself comfortable. Please be seated. Once again I'd like to thank you for your kind understanding that you had to be interposed by a witness whose health condition was not very good. So I hope you had a restful weekend. Today you will be asked questions by the accused, Mr. Radovan Karadzic, in his cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 2nd of April, you left Sarajevo and near Stjenice you were asked to produce your ID by soldiers from Sokolac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They knew that you were a Muslim and they probably wanted to know what it was that you had on you, but you were let pass, were you not?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You heard some sort of shooting. But before that, are you aware of a crisis of the 1st of March when a member of a wedding party was killed at Bascarsija?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is not contained in my statement either. Can you please ask me only on the issues I mentioned in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement of the 16th of November, 1994, at page 00070301, that thereafter you left for your village of Madjer, where you took part in the night watches. You say that you were not armed but that the situation was relatively peaceful. Can you tell us: How many of you were there in the group of individuals who stood guard?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the date, 16th of November, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The statement is dated the 16th of November, but it was on the 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that I went to the village of Madjer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 6th of April, you went to the village of Madjer.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you say that you kept a night watch, that it was relatively peaceful, that you only had a pistol; you didn't have that many weapons. Can you tell us how many of you were there and what was the name of the unit guarding Madjer?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was no sort of unit. The group included two or three members of each household. We would keep watch around our respective homes. That's what these watches were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Up until the 22nd of May, as you say, it was relatively calm. The neighbouring village of Leleci, a Serb village, was on good terms with you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that for four/six weeks after the war broke out in Sarajevo it was peaceful in your parts?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until the 22nd of May, no gun-fire could be heard. There was no fighting, no skirmishes. There was no sort of war to speak of up until the 22nd of May. On the 22nd of May, fire was opened on all these villages in the direction of Visegrad, namely Madjer, Kopljevici, Orahovo, Pokrivenik, Sredovcici [phoen], Cubrenik [phoen]. These were all villages close to my village, the village of Madjer. Shells were landing as well. It was the 22nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is Madjer a predominantly or fully a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a fully Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that it was envisaged that Madjer should form part of the Muslim municipality of Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 20th of May a young Serb policeman was killed while he was patrolling in a Serb village; they refused to hand over his body and said that they would do so only after they had killed ten more Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which village was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will look into that in a document later on. But do you know that the reason behind this conflict was the murder of a Serb policeman?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that point, you went to Radici and joined the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina under the command of Husein Hadzibulic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 2nd of May, I went there --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you perhaps come closer to the microphones. And perhaps both of us should wait for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 22nd of May, I was hiding about the village with my wife and two children, and in early June I went for the village of Radici. It was some 15 kilometres away from the village of Madjer. Sometime in mid-July we received a call - because there were many women, children, and elderly in the area, I already spoke about it - I received a call which said in a plain pencil that we should report to the village of Novakovici for a review of some sort. It may have been in mid-July, around the 20th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the unit under the command of Husein Hadzibulic, that particular unit?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: A commander was mentioned by the name of Agic. He was taken prisoner somewhere and was no longer present in the area. It was then said that Hadzibulic would be the commander. Mehemet Lubarda attended this particular review in the capacity of a commander. Now, this Hadzibulic was -- had a degree in economics and he only happened to be present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this Mehmet Agic who used to be in the Territorial Defence earlier on?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How big was that unit?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to that review, we had all been told to take all the weapons we had. When I arrived there, there were about 400 military-aged men. I did not know all of them because they came from Visegrad, because Visegrad had fallen at the time. There were refugees from Visegrad as well. And this Hadzibulic said to us that the persons who were armed should go on one side and those who are unarmed on the other side. There were about 400 of us, 400 men. About half were armed and the other half were not armed. These who were armed had hunting guns, then some M-48 rifles. There were also some automatic rifles, those who had fled from Rogatica. And that automatic -- those automatic rifles were the most serious weapons that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The village is called Zlatni Do, where the Serb policeman was killed. The young policeman's name was Mihajlovic. He patrolled the village and he was killed. His body was taken, and that caused a major dispute. Tell me, in that group were there certain groups, one headed by Selim Omeragic, another one included the Dzubro brothers, in the third one Hadzibulic's, then Enes Satrovic; do you know all of these people and did these groups actually exist either as battalions or companies?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Enes Satrovic, but I did not see him there. I don't remember that. He was a professor, if that's the man you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about this Omeragic, Dzubre?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know that, since I did not have any weapons, I was assigned to the work platoon, and I was digging trenches, as I've already mentioned, in the village of Salakovici. That is what the name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Djubre, you don't know?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that last name. Djubre?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Or Cubre.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cubre, that does exist, but I don't know anything about them. They are from the village of Cubric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't know anything about them?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm a bit perplexed here, Mr. Hurko. Look at paragraph -- paragraph 14 -- sorry, paragraph 6 of your statement. You say: "I had to go to the village of Mazar [as interpreted] to get food." Maybe it's a question of translation; the translation is: "I was forced to go." Is it not right to say "I was supposed to go," or did someone force you to go?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody forced me. I was supposed to go. I had to go because we didn't have any food for the children or anything. We had this wheat and then it was ripe and a few days earlier on my father would go and pick this wheat. On the 14th of August, I went to try to help him bring this wheat so that we would have food. I wasn't forced. I was supposed to. I had to go. Should -- it says here I was forced, and that means forced.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So where were you when you went to Madjer?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where was I?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the village of Radic, above --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were in a unit?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No unit. I was in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All the time from when you reported to this unit until your arrest in 14 -- on the 14th of August until you were taken prisoner were you in the military?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in the military. I was in a work platoon, and I was digging trenches and roads. And I don't have a single hour in the military, and I can show you my military booklet by way of a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you get this certificate for privatisation? What does it say there?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What privatisation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you receive a certificate? I'm sure that you received a certificate, either as a citizen or as a retiree or as a participant in the war. All citizens received certificates. Now, what kind of certificate did you receive?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian victim of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at this. You say: "I set out to the village with Ahmet Cubro" --

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ahmet Cubro joined me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you confused me when you said that you didn't know anything about them. So you do know something after all, do you?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And he was in this unit; right?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He was in the woods, just like I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Hurko, what happened in that period between the 10th and 14th August when you were taken prisoner? Do you know --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, can we look at 1D04158.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that your unit attacked the village of Pljesko and that the attack was led by Selim Omeragic and Kasim Velic, who was a captain, and they torched Serb houses, Alem Hasacic [phoen]; Zagorica Mujez [phoen], nicknamed Sef; and Rusmir Balas, nicknamed Koljac, the butcher? Did you know all that?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 10th of August, my father went to the village of Madjer to get that wheat. I was in the village of Radic in the woods with my children. And on the 14th of August I set off. I don't know anything about these operations. I was not there, I wasn't -- I don't know who organised this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have a look at this document. Paragraph 6 now, please, so it would be the next page. And then another part of your unit at the same time burned the village of Kozici. The inhabitants fled, so there were no victims, but the village of Kozici was razed to the ground. Do you know that this was the Cubro clan that did that, then Senaid, Sead, Sarija, and Nazif, then Dzananovici and Adem Imsirevic. Please look at paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, Karadzic, you mention this unit of mine. I was not in the army. Do you understand that? I don't know what the army was doing and what they burned and when they burned it. I don't know anything about that. With my children or with my wife, I was in the woods. If you wish, I can tell you what it was like and what the woods were like and who the women and children were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see that you say that in your statement of the 16th of November, 1994, on this same page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not get the number of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this is what you said. I'm going to read it out in English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you upload it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Excuse me, could I just raise one point: Earlier we were looking at 1D04158, which is not on the list of documents provided by the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we dealt with it with the previous witness, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Oh, is that right. Okay. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably he forgot to raise it -- to tender that. We may need Ms. Edgerton, but I think we can come -- Was it your intention to tender that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, certainly. But it doesn't matter. This witness will do as well, because this has to do with what happened in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your statement of the 16th of November, 1994. Page number is 91 -- 3091 -- I actually have something different. My numbers are different. The second paragraph: "That is when we decided to go to another village further away from Rogatica. I set out together with my family. I went to the village of Radici, above Ustipraca, where we hid in the forest," I think, "I joined the TO unit of the RBiH, whose commander was Husein Hadzibulic. He lined us all up and since we did not have enough weapons, he deployed me and the work platoon. As a member of the work platoon, I dug trenches ..." and so on. Now, is it correct that you were in this unit under the command of Husein Hadzibulic, if that's how you pronounce it?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that I was there for the line up, for the review, that was on the 20th of July, 1992. I had time to dig these trenches and build roads, and I was taken prisoner on the 14th of August. So it didn't last for more than 20-odd days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But, Mr. Hurko, work platoon, it is a platoon, it's a military formation, isn't it, and it is within this unit? And your commander was Husein Hadzibulic. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time no one knew anything, what was command, who was commanding. I was just digging these roads towards Ustipraca. Nothing was set up, Territorial Defence, whatever; all of that happened after I was taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us see what it says here further on, that your father came across Ramiz Alajbegovic, the former deputy commander of the Rogatica station, and on that occasion Ramiz Alajbegovic gave my father a laissez-passer and at the same time asked him to arrange a meeting with people from Lelek for him; right? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He gave him some kind of pass, because they no longer allowed us to go back to this Madjer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then your father was given the task of arranging contacts with Leleci with the intention of having Leleci come to the side of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he arrived in Madjer, he met someone from Leleci and he said that Ramiz Alajbegovic and somebody else wanted to meet with these people from Leleci, and then they, along with my father, met with these people from Leleci; that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And Leleci -- it seems not everything has been recorded in the transcript. Now it has been recorded, I guess. Then Mr. Izetbegovic was trying to persuade the people from Leleci to join the Territorial Defence, which was later the source of your trouble; right?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of trouble?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that held against you, when the Serbs took you prisoner?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They met and Ramiz asked them whether they would like to join the Territorial Defence, and they said no, they were waging war against the Muslims. And that was it. That was the only thing they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they not say this is a war between the Serbs and the Muslims and everyone should be with their own people?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there you go. You can put it that way as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You did your military service, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can it be said, roughly, that the army consists of personnel and materiel?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is there in the military apart from personnel and materiel?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the quarter-masters corps. I have a bit of training. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You confirmed in paragraph 5 that you saw this order of Rajko Kusic in which he said to all units that personnel was being destroyed without hesitation. That is what is stated here, and that's the translation: "Personnel," it said there; whereas they use the word "ziva sila," manpower?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really do not understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 5 of your amalgamated statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please slow down. I take it there is no B/C/S translation for his amalgamated statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No, there isn't. A very large part of his amalgamated statement are, in fact, based on this Bosnian statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you confirmed that you saw an order of Rajko Kusic, one that he issued to his troops, to destroy personnel, manpower, without any hesitation. What did it say there, "manpower" or "personnel"?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where I saw that. I don't know where I said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For your convenience, I read out your amalgamated statement, Mr. Hurko. So paragraph 5 of your amalgamated statement reads as follows: "I have also been shown a copy of a document dated 23rd of May, 1992 -- " In the meantime, we'll upload it. "... which appears to be issued by Rajko Kusic, ordering units to hold their positions in certain villages in Rogatica municipality and ordering the mopping-up of Oskoplje, Kusturice, Zakoma, and Kalimanici. Oskoplje, Kusturice, and Kalimanici are Muslim. Zakoma is mixed. In this, he orders that 'all units are to carry out destruction of personnel without hesitation.' This document is consistent with what I saw: There was an attack on many Muslim villages in Rogatica municipality on 22nd May 1992 and the following days." This is what you state in your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what was shown to me, this document. This document was shown to me here in The Hague. I did not give that as my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you said that is consistent with what you saw.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was shown to me, I saw it, and it corresponds to what happened on that day, at the end where I was, those people shooting at those villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So Mr. Karadzic's question was that there's a passage in that document which says "all units are to carry out destruction of personnel without hesitation." So his question was whether that passage was consistent with what you saw, whether you have anything to say in relation to that passage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what they meant by "ziva sila," "personnel." Women, children, old men, everybody was there. Women were delivering babies. And they call all of them personnel, manpower? They shelled this entire area. I don't understand what they mean by "personnel," "manpower."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they have any prisoners? Were you taken prisoner, killed?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me? Was I taken prisoner or killed? I was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But the destruction of personnel or manpower, is that what you saw? Is that what personnel refers to in military terminology? Does it refer to soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were civilians and soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How can a civilian be personnel or manpower? Where have you found that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We need to put a pause and slow down. Yes, we can proceed. Can you answer the question, Mr. Hurko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot answer this question. I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For them you are personnel. You were not killed, but you were imprisoned; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, I wasn't killed. I was captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you were asked by this gentleman, Pecanica, if you are armed, and he ordered them not to beat you, and he informed you that from that point on you are a prisoner; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you answered that you are not armed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said I didn't have weapons, that my children were left behind in the village of Radovo. I asked them to let me go back to my children. He said, no, you have to go back to the village of Kosovo, that I would be questioned by Rajko Kusic, and that they would release me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then they found 70 bullets in your pocket; correct?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You did not report the bullets or you didn't manage to dispose of them?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I couldn't. I was afraid. How could I throw them away?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You had a licence for your pistol. Did you have a licence to carry a pistol and 70 bullets, or did you have a licence to possess a pistol?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: To possess a pistol. I don't know about the bullets. I bought them in shops before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that a permit for carrying a gun does not also mean that you would be permitted to take a gun out of your house?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And against whom, at whom, were you supposed to fire those 70 bullets?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At nobody. I had them in war time and peace time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Please slow down. Because of the overlap, the interpreters were not able to catch what you said in answer to the question whether you knew that a permit for carrying a gun does not also mean that you would be permitted to take a gun out of your house. How did you answer that question, Mr. Hurko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since it was war time, I carried what I could carry from my house. So I took the pistol from my house. I couldn't leave it behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And those 70 bullets were intended for Serbs or for somebody else?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not intended for anyone, not Serbs, not anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that Serb villages in Rogatica were torched on a daily basis and if there were inhabitants still in the villages, they were killed?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hurko, is it correct that from the 22nd -- from the 20th of May until the 14th of August Serbian villages were attacked and torched every day and Serb civilians were killed?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. You are just making that up now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Is it correct that each Muslim village had its own TO unit?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each village, each village before the war guarded their homes for as long as they could. Then when they couldn't, they would take their wives and children and run. You keep skipping over the question. First you ask me about the village of Kosovo, and when I was talking to Pecanica, I was supposed to complete that segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I will ask that at the end. We will come to that, to the swallowing of the bullets and all of that.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: And about Pecanica who arrested me, I just wanted to talk about that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I can see that you changed a lot about names, such as the word "Chetnik," but some of that stayed in the paragraph. So I'm interested to know what you mean when you say "Chetnik." We have that in paragraph 8, 7, paragraph 8 and 9, and all -- so on, 10. What is a "Chetnik" to you? You can say whatever you want. Nobody will get angry. Are these bearded men with some insignia or do you refer to all Serbs as Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all Serbs, no. More it would be those men with the beards and the cockades, I think that's what they're called, skull and cross-bones insignia on their caps, and they would kill people in Rogatica. When they came to the prison, they would beat us up. I call them Chetniks. We all call them Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit the document that was on the screen, 1D04158, although we will call it up several times more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You haven't asked a question in relation to this current witness. Is it your intention based upon what you discussed with the previous witness to tender that into evidence? Or you are minded to ask some questions in relation to this document to Mr. Hurko?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did. I did. Can we have it again? Yes, here it is. Can we then see these paragraphs. Can we then have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can I observe at this stage, before we get any further: We have no real idea what this document is. The previous witness has confirmed nothing about this document, and this document should be treated with extreme care by the Trial Chamber, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is -- has an ERN number. It was evidently placed into the EDS by the OTP. The document was evidently seized somewhere, and it is full of -- well, it provides an overview of events and pertains to this witness until the 14th of August, and we can see here what was happening on the 23rd of June, houses were burned in Solakovica, where Dzananovic Mustafa particularly excelled, Djedovic Alija, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not for you to give evidence. It's for you to put questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, can you look at this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is this page? Can we ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page because at the time you were not in Rogatica before the conflict broke out, before April. Can we look at the next page, please. Do you know where the Serbian village of Vodice is, and do you know that it was destroyed on the 5th of July?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Selo Vodice. I know where it is, generally. And I know that it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know Milomir Obradovic was a casualty there, his daughter was raped and killed, his son Danko, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear of some people. Now I don't know what their names are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know about the village of Starcici, where eight Serb houses were burned on the 23rd of June?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand if the witness said yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of Rusmir Balas, aka Koljac, the butcher?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where the Koljac nickname comes from. I knew Rusmir Balas from before the war. I knew he was a waiter in Rogatica, And I did not see him in that area. And once again I say: I was not a soldier. I had two small children, aged 7 and 10. I was in the forest with my wife most of the time. And when I did join, I was digging some road a few occasions, and I was digging trenches once. So I really don't know much about the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hurko, I'm not accusing you of anything, God forbid. All I want is for us to clarify with your help what was happening there. Here, paragraph 8, please pay attention. In mid-August, the village of Kozice was burned by Cubre with his unit - Cubro, Sead; Cubro, Senaid; Cubro, Sarija; Cubro, Nazif, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mid-August?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I was arrested in the -- on the 14th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this was in mid-August, the 12th and the 13th.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in July, near the location of Saran, an ambush was set up and Rajak Dragoljub and Bosko Ljubinac were killed in a car?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I passed by Saran only once and I didn't see anything. I was digging trenches on the other side, and Radici's completely in a different area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit it now? It seems the witness does know something.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I will observe, Mr. President, that the document is not signed, it's not stamped, it's not dated. What the witness has had to say on the document is on the transcript. In my submission, it doesn't meet the threshold for showing the indicia for authenticity and reliability that are normally present.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a signature "A. Jesic" on the first page. "A. Jesic." There is a signature on the first page and there is an ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So your submission is that this is the signature of the author of this document, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an overview, a report, and it was drafted by Mr. Jesic. If it's necessary, we can MFI it. But this was not something that was obtained by the Defence. It was something that was already there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Prosecution is not sure about this -- the authenticity about this document, although the previous witness recognised some individuals referred to in the report and some matters are concerned with contemporaneous matters, but we didn't have sufficient basis to admit this document through the previous two witnesses. You will have another opportunity to call witness to -- through whom you can tender this document, but not at this time. We will not admit this, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you describe seeing Rajko Kusic once and that you knew that it was Rajko Kusic because he told you so, and does that mean that you didn't know him from before?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know Rajko Kusic from before. But it was like this: When I was arrested - you mentioned this Pecanica - they brought me to the village of Kosovo, which was on the ... and then on the right-hand side there, there was Mico Andric and garage --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we will deal with that later.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just tell you something about Rajko Kusic. This is where I met him. He introduced himself. May I say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll do it later. I just want to ask you this: Do you know that others also introduced themselves as Rajko Kusic?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D04161.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: This, again, is a document which is not on the list of documents notified to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the reason being what, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the reason is the pace. We cannot have time for everything. It's just a statement. We're not going to tender it. Just -- it's for purposes of testifying to this fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We postponed your cross-examination of this witness for your convenience, and I think you should have been able to give your notice to the Prosecution at least. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, if you can look at line 15 from the bottom, it says: Kosovo an officer who introduced himself at the time as Kusic Rajko, which I could see for myself that it wasn't Kusic Rajko because I knew Kusic personally, so I said nothing, I said nothing -- oh, I lost my place. So I said nothing and accepted his false introduction.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that is not true. I know this just as if it happened yesterday, and I already told you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, just this question: Do you know that different people introduced themselves with different names and that some people who were not Rajko Kusic introduced themselves as Rajko Kusic?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hurko, could you repeat your answer, kindly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was brought into the village of Kosovo, there were four soldiers who entered that garage. These soldiers that brought us in, they were professional, they didn't beat us or mistreat us. When we entered the garage, we sat on a bench or something over there. It was my father, my mother, and my cousin Abdulah, and myself. Four soldiers entered. This one who was there who had a moustache. I didn't know Rajko Kusic from before the war. He said, Do you know me? We said, No, we don't know. He said, I'm Rajko Kusic, the commander of the Serbian army in Roga-- and then after that he said, Have you heard of me? And then we said, Yes, we have, we're glad ... and so on and so forth. And then he said that Stojan Perkovic -- Perkovic and Krsmanovic, please search them. He called them by name. Then they came up to us, they searched us, they put pistols in our mouths, they made me eat the bullets. He hit me on the head with the ammunition. He made me eat three bullets. If Karadzic doesn't believe that, that man can confirm that. He confirmed that in Sarajevo, that I was forced to eat those bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for an hour. In the meantime, I wonder, Mr. Robinson, if you could have a word with Mr. Karadzic whether he needs to put a third party's statement which is not likely to be admitted in order to put some information to the witness. We'll resume at 1.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me examine one aspect of this. The soldiers did not beat you up?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Pecanica knew me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was he their superior officer or a person of some importance?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was just an ordinary soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But he did have the authority to ask of them not to beat you?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was in passing, as they were taking us over there. He didn't say anything. He didn't say that we should be either beaten or not, but they did not beat us as we were on our way to that garbage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, in paragraph 7 you say Pecanica told the others not to beat you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were taken prisoner perhaps he told the others that he knew me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is one thing that I find worrisome, Mr. Hurko: You have never seen your statement in our own language, have you?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The final amalgamated statement you signed a day or two ago. Was it all in English, or did you have a copy in Serbian or Bosnian, as you will?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they read it back to me in Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 11 you say that Kusic ordered that you be taken out in order that he may interrogate you. You say that he did not interrogate you for long about the deployment of your forces and the strength of your troops. Were you able to give him any information at all?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As he was interrogating me, Perkovic and Bra na Krsmanovic would beat me. They would beat me and my father in turns. As soon as they put a question to me and I started answering, they would stat beating me up. So there wasn't anything specific until -- or any of the occasions that I was taken out during my stay in the garage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, Kusic did ask that you be singled out this once, and then he told the others that they should not beat you up?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the only one singled out and taken out of the garage by Kusic. There was this other individual who was there with a rifle --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Kusic said: No, we're not interested in what you're telling us; we're interested in something else. He then went on to say that Darko Neric should go to the garage and tell the others that they should not beat my father. Neric went to the garage first, I followed, and Kusic was behind me. And as I got into the garage, I saw my father on the floor, both of his ears cut up, all blooded over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. So you were not beaten up as soon as you were taken prisoner. It was only when they found these bullets on you that they started beating you up and forced you to swallow them?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they started beating us up right away. It didn't have anything to do with the bullets. As they were beating us up, Stojan Perkovic found these bullets in my pocket. But the beating started up right -- started right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This isn't what you stated in your statement, sir.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Is this the only time you were forced to swallow bullets?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it also happened at the prison in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me that I was going to swallow all the bullets they had, but I couldn't swallow more than three. At some point as I was in the prison, Vinko Bulic also forced me to swallow bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that in the school building certain Muslims were singled out who were considered to be loyal and they were sent home; right?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we got to the school building in Rogatica, Kusic knocked on the door of this high school building and a Muslim opened the door. He was the one who answered the door. It was all Muslims who were in the camp. They told me that my mother, my father, and I should go upstairs, and then he proceeded to say that my father would be -- would stay there and my mother and I would proceed somewhere else. This was on the same day, the 14th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it not true that your mother asked to be taken with you as you were taken prisoner in your village?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it not true that Sosa, Hodzic, and some other Muslims were called out; they said that they pledged their allegiance to them, and they were released?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the following day, on the 16th, in the morning when a truck arrived with a tarp and all of us were told to board that bus, save for the Sosa and Hodzic families and some others who were believed to be loyalists and were allowed to go home. So everybody was forced aboard that bus, save for my mother and I. But the Basic family was killed in 1993 in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there existed at least five villages in Rogatica which were loyal and continued living there normally until the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Satorovici, Tmurni Do, Kosovo, and a place called Burati, for those I know for a fact that they stayed there. Whether they were loyal or not, they were all transferred to Sarajevo in 1994. I -- I took the belongings that the Serbs were taking out of their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it not true that they laid their arms down and were free to leave whenever they wished to, not necessarily before the Dayton Accords were signed?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were exchanged on the 6th of October, 1994, together with me. They were all transferred to Sarajevo as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Things did not happen that way, but anyway we'll see a document to that effect soon. As for the beatings, is my understanding correct that it was those who knew you from before who beat you the most; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it applied to those who we knew and those who we didn't know. I didn't know Rajko Kusic. As for Stojan Perkovic, I knew him by sight. I knew that he worked at the Elektrodistribucija in Rogatica. Krsmanovic, also known as Pipa, is someone I didn't know but who beat me up on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This person Dida [phoen] did not beat you up at the SUP in Rogatica, did he?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, who is this Dida? I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 27 of your statement: "On that day, a man by the name of Dida, an inspector of the SUP in Rogatica."

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not "Dida," "Djida."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Right. Is he a Serb or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He was only putting questions and he was not beating anyone up.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He interrogated my father outside the prison and did not beat him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we call in e-court -- can we have 1D04166, please. 1D04166.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I want to note for the record, again, that this was not on the list of documents provided to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm expecting to hear something from you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was notified in respect of the earlier witness and this particular municipality. I can't possibly do it for every witness. I was meaning to use it with the earlier witness, but I was not given the time. Is it not true that the document was notified in respect of the earlier witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, let us proceed this time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at this agenda of the meeting of the Executive Committee. The date is the 6th of September, 1992. And it says here that the only item on the agenda is the provision and supply of essential foodstuffs to the residents of the villages of Satorovici, Okruglo, Tmurni Do. And also Loburati [phoen] should be added to this; it's a place in the direction of Sokolac, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the conclusions at the bottom. The Muslim population in the villages of Satorovici, Okruglo, Tmurni Do, and Osovo shall be assigned the essential foodstuffs, namely flour, macaroni, rice, sugar, cooking oil, coffee, salt, et cetera, according to the criteria laid down by the Executive Committee relating to the provision of essential foodstuffs to other inhabitants of Rogatica municipality." Were you aware, Mr. Witness, that they were equated in every respect to the Serbs, that they -- the Serbian authorities paid them visits, that they stayed there for as long as they wished, and that none of them were killed?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them were killed. I was a prisoner at the time, and I was unable to be aware of any of this. I was going through the greatest of suffering.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was killed?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sejfo Mirvic was killed in mid-December in the prison in Rogatica. He was one of the loyalists from Satorovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll see what happened on that occasion. We have it in your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I don't believe the witness has added a great deal to the document itself, but I'll leave it in Your Honours' discretion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He is aware of these villages, he did enumerate them, including Burati.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The fact that he knows certain villages referred to in the document does not mean that that document can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, he is aware of the fact that the villages were leading a peaceful life, that they were treated equally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. How would I be able to know if they received food or not? I said that I was in the prison in Rogatica at the time. I wasn't able to know what they were doing. I didn't even know who stayed behind as a loyalist. This was something I learned later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And was it later on that you learned that these villages had not been attacked and had not been set on fire; right?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The villages had not been set on fire, because when individuals were brought over to Rogatica from these villages, they were forced to board buses and were then taken to Rogatica. This was in 1993. All of them were rounded up and taken to the Rogatica prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is not true. Witness, you just stated -- I put it to you that some of them stayed even after the Dayton Accords and everyone stayed for as long as they wished. Look at 1994/1993; do you claim that these villages were attacked and people arrested?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In November of 1993, all of the people from these villages were taken to Rogatica, to a separate hut as part of the prison. And when the attack ensued on Gorazde, all the able-bodied persons were carrying food, and I was among them. They were all carrying food to Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is inaccurate, not true, and I will prove it.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You do that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I leave it in the hands of the Trial Chamber. I do believe that this should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber does not see any basis to admit this document through this witness, Mr. Karadzic. It's time to -- for you to conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you mentioned that Mirvic had been killed. In this statement did you omit to mention what you mentioned earlier on, namely that the MUP had carried out an investigation and that this Bojic, or whoever, had lied to them, to the effect that Mirvic was killed as he was trying to escape?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember it was a Friday, and all of these people from the village of Satorovici were sent to take a bath --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Wait a second. We're talking about Milici.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you once again: During the night, in Vinko's office there was some noise, some banging, and we heard that. And in the morning, when we were supposed to go to work, Vinko walked in about 8.00 or 9.00 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can no longer hear the witness due to background noise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hurko, I apologise. Because of the noise I made, the interpreters were not able to hear you. Could you kindly repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a Friday evening. Vinko Bojic, the prison warden, had sent all form Satorovici to the village to take a bath and then he said he'd return them the next day. That evening, in Vinko's office, there was some noise, banging, in Vinko's office. You could hear some banging, and we did not know what was going on. In the morning, around 8.00 or 9.00, Vinko came and said, Imagine this Mirvic tried to escape and my guards caught up with him and killed him. Within 15 minutes' time a doctor came, whom I had known before the war, he came wearing a white coat, and he went to Mirvic's body. When this doctor came and went back, within 15 minutes' time, he let us go and bury Mirvic in our own way - how do I put it? - in the Muslim way. And then some people went to dig the grave and others were cutting something up there and I walked up to the body then. He was wearing a sweater and jeans. I could not recognise his face at all. It was beyond recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you say that the MUP had carried out an on-site investigation and that he had said to them that this Mirvic -- or rather, that he had lied?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was probably a mistake. I corrected it here one day. I said that it was a doctor, not the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You did say that it was a doctor -- no, the MUP.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said when I made the statement that it may have been a mistake. It was either me or the typist or whoever. But I corrected it when I came here on Thursday, I think it was. It was the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These people who mistreated you, was anybody held accountable, this Perkovic, for instance?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was before a court in Sarajevo and I was a witness there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know or do you agree that the mosque in the centre of Rogatica was renewed, restored, with the support of the Serb authorities, the municipal authorities, and the Government of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me tell you that both of the mosques that used to be in Rogatica were razed to the ground, and we prisoners had to clean all of that up. Who restored them after the war, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I please have 1D04176. That is Mr. Perkovic's judgement. It is a final decision before the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you testify in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure that that transcript had been disclosed to us, but I'm not going to create any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Let me just clarify the position. Mr. Hurko's transcript of evidence before the court in Bosnia and Herzegovina was disclosed on the 5th of July, 2011, having been received by the Prosecution on the 22nd of June, 2011.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly. Can we have a look at pages 2 and 3 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at paragraph 3. Sefik Hurko -- does it say here that he was found guilty because he took part in the unlawful detention of civilians Fejzo Hurko, Sefik Hurko, Abdulah Hurko, and Izo [as interpreted] Hurko, and also physical maltreatment and humiliation of Sefik Hurko, and the bullets are referred to here. Do you know that he was found guilty of that?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I know about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was found guilty of everything that he had done, that he was sentenced to 12 years, and that he admitted that guilt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He admitted that he had done all of that?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He admitted all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did he mention a reason? Was it personal vengeance or whatever?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean reasons?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did he say why he had behaved that way?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was closed session. They closed the court session and he said why he made us eat bullets and why he behaved that way. So they discussed that behind closed doors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise. I really do not have any ill-will towards you. I'm just trying to realise why someone had done something, and I'm trying to establish the facts. I have respect for you, and I am sorry about everything that you've experienced.

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I say something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hurko.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the killings Becir -- Musevic, Adil, Najl, Alija Omerhodzic, Mirsad Omanovic, you did not ask me anything about all of that and I don't know why you didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We are going to deal with that through other witnesses, Mr. Hurko. I was interested in what you knew and saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor, do you have any questions for --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Just one point of clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: It was a question put by Mr. Karadzic which was at the end of page 84 of today's proceedings. He said: "These people who mistreated you, was anyone held accountable, Perkovic, for instance?" You said, Mr. Hurko, your answer was: "He was before a court in Sarajevo and I was a witness there, yes." Could you clarify the year that you were a witness in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SEFIK HURKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: 2009. I think it was the 15th of October, 2009.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's the only question I have. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hurko, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber and the Tribunal, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please have a safe journey home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The next witness is Mr. Amir [sic] Bazdar. While he's coming in, Mr. President, I want to point out, first of all, myself and Mr. Robinson have agreed that the testimony of Mr. Bazdar was disclosed to the Defence on the 5th of July, 2011, having been received by the Prosecution on the 22nd of June, 2011. It was the same batch of disclosure as Mr. Hurko's evidence. The second point is: Could we have five minutes at the end of the witness's evidence to make an oral application, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I can confirm that we did in fact receive it, and I can only apologise and tell you really we don't know what we have because we have so much material. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this judgement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this judgement from Sarajevo? Can I have it admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: There's no objection from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't see any problem. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1665, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Probably it was -- and I will deal with this. Good afternoon, sir. Do you hear me in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
