utterances.text: Before we hear the evidence of this witness, probably I asked you whether -- how we should deal with the witness statement of the previous witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I saw the transcript in relation to that. My proposal was to speak to the witness, now that he has concluded his evidence, to see what his position on the matter is and then to revert to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, could you state your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: My name is Armin Bazdar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: I'm a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could I call up, please, 65 ter 07472.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is it correct that you provided a statement to investigators of this Tribunal which you signed on the 23rd of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to go through that statement yesterday in detail and to identify a number of corrections which you wished to make to it before you adopt it as your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to go through the corrections which you have identified and to ask you to make two clarifications which you've identified. At page 2, the last paragraph: The words "they knew the war was going to break out" should read "they believed the war was going to break out." Page 3, second paragraph: "I know that the JNA had" should read "I heard that the JNA had ." Page 3, fourth paragraph: The date "April 4th, 1992" should read "3rd June, 1992" --

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: I do apologise. Could you just slow down a bit so that I can follow this. It's tiny and you're moving so fast through all of this. Could you just slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I can indeed. Mr. Witness, I can assure you that these are the changes that you have already informed us of, but if there is any --

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Okay, but -- well, fine. But just do slow down so that I can follow all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you go one by one so that the witness can follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Would you like me to begin at the beginning, Witness?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: You don't have to. You can go on now. You can go on from where you stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Witness, in your statement it says "there was one man killed during this attack on our village." That's, in the English, page 3, in the fourth paragraph. I believe it's the third paragraph, last sentence, on the version which appears on the left, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Is it correct you want to clarify that the man who was killed was a Muslim civilian called Becir Ramovic?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Yes, I just wanted to say that because that was not written in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If we could go, now, to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Sixth paragraph in English. I'm going to read the relevant words. You said "members of the White Eagles," and you wish to change that to read "members of the White Eagles and local Serbs."

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness because of background noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, please, Witness.

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Page 4, sixth paragraph. It refers to "buses and trucks." You wish to correct that to read "one bus and three trucks." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Page 4, the seventh paragraph in English. It said "I was young, only 14," you wish that to read "I was young, only 15."

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Page 4, the eighth paragraph. It refers to "two offices"; you wish that to read "two rooms"?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The original reads "two offices." We're talking about a place where you were placed in R asadnik. Your original says "we were placed in two offices with no furniture"; you wish it to read "we were placed in two rooms with no furniture"?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. However, this also has to do with interpretation. A moment ago the interpreter said "two officers," not "two offices." But what you said just now is correct. So there are these translation and interpretation issues. I don't know who this is who is interpreting this, but this person said "two officers" instead of "two offices." So instead of saying that I wanted to say "two rooms" rather than "two offices," this person said "rather than two officers." I really don't know why this kind of thing happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. The correction is clear. Thank you. Page 5, paragraph 5. It refers to a woman called Neda, N-e-d-a; is it correct that her name is in fact Nada, as appears in paragraph 3?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Page 5, the fifth -- the fifth paragraph. It says that you were -- you got out by the front line near a shelter. Is it correct that you wish to change that to a "naturally sheltered area," rather than "shelter"?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Page 6, paragraph 1, you referred to a Serb named Spiro. Is it correct that you were referring to a Serb whose nickname is Spiro, whose real name is Dragoje Paunovic?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Page 6, the second paragraph. The original says "I managed to speak with my uncle for a few minutes ..." you wish that to read "I managed to speak with my uncle for a few seconds."

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And the fifth paragraph on page 6, where you give an account of the execution, you wish to add that 24 Muslim male civilians were executed in that incident. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Page 7, fourth paragraph. I want to draw your attention to the sequence in which it is stated in your statement and then I wish to invite you to make whatever correction you wish. This refers to after you separated from Ago Kapo. You said: "We separated. I walked about 18 hours in the woods. I hid along the way. On this night, the Serbs did see me and fired at me. I was crawling on my hands and knees. I was lucky enough not to get shot again. I managed to hide myself under leaves. The Serbs never found me." Would you care to clarify the sequence of events.

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Yes, of course I'll do that. When we separated, I hid below -- underneath some leaves in order to move on, hoping to get away from the execution site. After that, a group of these Serbs saw me, these Serbs who had returned to the execution site. They opened fire at me. One of them actually ran after me hoping to catch me. Then I continued crawling across this meadow. After that, I stood up and fled into the nearby forest. So then comes the rest; namely, that I wandered around the forest for 18 hours until I reached the line of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That would be roughly a summary of that paragraph that was not in the right chronological order. So there are no significant changes apart from this chronology.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: In your statement on the same page, at paragraphs 4 and 5, this is page 7, there is a reference to "Muslim Territorial Defence." Is it correct that you wish that to read "Bosnia and Herzegovina Territorial Defence"?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: You give an account in the fifth paragraph on this page - and I believe it's the next page in B/C/S, please - of the verification by the TO forces that you were a Muslim and that they gave you first aid. I believe that you wish to clarify the sequence in which you were provided with first aid and the manner of verification. Do you wish to do that?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: You've already said that yourself. If necessary, I shall clarify. But you have put it right just now. If necessary, I can explain further.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Please just explain in a few sentences. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Very well. When I reached this line that was under the control of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the first thing that happened was that I was given first aid. Since I had been wounded in both hands and arms. I had four holes in my hands and arms, exit/entry wounds due to the execution that had taken place on the previous day. After that, the soldiers of the Territorial Defence of the BH told me to unbutton my trousers so that they would be able to ascertain whether I was a Muslim or not, namely, whether I had been circumcised. I don't know what the word you use is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Subject to the corrections which you've made and the clarifications that you've made, do you adopt that statement as your evidence? And if you were asked questions on the same subjects today, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I tender that statement, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3286, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, I now propose to read a summary of the statement for the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. Bazdar is a Bosnian Muslim from the village of Seljani in Rogatica municipality. On 4th April 1992, the hamlet of Ovlagije, which is near Seljani, was shelled. Following the attack, Serb soldiers rounded up Muslim inhabitants in Seljani and held them under a form of house arrest for four months. On 4th of August, 1992, Serb soldiers transported the Muslim villagers in groups to the Veljko Vlahovic secondary school in Rogatica, where other non-Serb inhabitants from Seljani were already detained. Mr. Bazdar spent one night at the school. During the course of that night, he heard females screaming and crying. He was later told that women were raped at the school. On 5th of August, 1992, White Eagles and local Serbs separated the military-aged men from the women and children. The women and children were loaded onto buses and trucks and transported from Rogatica for exchange. Mr. Bazdar was taken with other Muslim males to Rasadnik, where he was instructed to clean vacated Muslim apartments which were to be used by Serbs. On 15th August 1992, Serb soldiers took Mr. Bazdar and other detainees to the front line in Duljevac, where a number of detainees were used by Serb soldiers as human shields. Subsequently, a Serb soldier, Dragoje Paunovic, known as Spiro, ordered that the group of approximately 27 Muslim males be killed. Mr. Bazdar and two other detainees survived the execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bazdar, I want to take you to the 15th of August, 1992. How old were you on that day?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: On that day I was 15 years old, 15 years, one month, and ten days, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Do you believe that you were the only person in the group taken for execution who was aged under the age of 18?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: No, there were others who were younger than 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Would you be able to give your best estimate as to how many others?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: No, I cannot state that with any certainty. And I wouldn't like to speculate, since I didn't know all of those people from before. So perhaps there were about five of us, up to five. But please don't rely on that as completely accurate. But I think that that was how many of us there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I want to take you to the moment when Mustafa Tankovic and Hamdija Jasarevic said they were injured. Do you recall that moment?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: I do remember, but I would just like to draw your attention. I am following the translation, the transcript what you're reading. It's not the 4th of April, 1992, when the attack occurred at the beginning of your -- well, this document that you're reading now. Yesterday I clarified that it wasn't the 4th of April, but it's the 3rd of June. So at the very beginning when you were presenting this document - I don't know what it's called ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In any event, the summary Mr. Gaynor just read is not part of the evidence. He just introduced the summary of your evidence which was written in your statement for the benefit of the public. In any event, thank you very much for your clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Apologies for not correcting the summary. Now, I'd like to take you to the moment that I've just described, where Mustafa Tankovic and Hamdija Jasarevic said they were injured. Could you describe the sequence of events after that moment.

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: After that, the sequence of events was as follows: People were being taken away as human shields. Among them was Mustafa Tankovic and Hamdija Jasarevic who were wounded. After they were brought back from being used as human shields with the other civilians, the Muslims who were there, I joined them and a number of other people who did not go to be used as human shields. And when we joined them, I was standing next to my uncle. Since our hands were tied behind our backs individually, each one of us had their hands tied behind their back, I touched my uncle with my elbow and asked him, "Where are they taking us now?" He told me quietly that it was all over for us and that we were going to be killed. After that, Dragoje Paunovic, called Spiro, came with those people who were returning from being used as human shields and ordered one of the soldiers, one of the Serb soldiers, to take us where he said we were to go. This Serb soldier went where this guy told him to go. And then from the place where we joined up, where I joined the group with some other people, where we joined the people who were returning from being used as human shields, he took us to a meadow and ordered the soldier to stop. In the meantime, he turned to us, Dragoje Paunovic, aka Spiro, and asked if there were any among us who were wounded. Hamdija Jasarevic spoke up, as well as Mustafa Tankovic. And then Spiro said, Just the two of you? He was surprised and noted this: Do you know how many of our people have been killed or wounded? When the soldier who was going in front of us approached, Spiro ordered him to kill us. The soldier passed by him cold-bloodedly, cocked his automatic rifle, and started to kill the men one by one, starting at the back of the column, as we were coming from the direction of that point where we all joined up. At that point, since there were younger people among us, as young as I was and a little bit older ones, some spoke up and said: Please, uncle, don't; what have we done to you? And then at that point Dragoje Paunovic, aka Spiro, cocked his automatic rifle and began to fire bursts of fire at us. That's when I was hit in my left forearm. I fell with my face to the ground. My uncle was standing on my left side just before the shooting began, and after these bursts of fire, when I fell, he fell next to me. And his head fell on my right hand or arm. I heard him gurgling, drowning in his own blood. It was evident that he was shot in the area of his chest and the lungs. And after the execution, I saw that that indeed was so. That was when I decided to stand up and try to escape, because I saw that my uncle was bleeding from the mouth, from his nostrils, and from his ears. Perhaps I changed the sequence, but I will try to explain that. After the bursts of fire were over and the executions were done, there was individual shooting, I assume at those people who were still showing signs of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, sir, Mr. Bazdar, could I ask you to come to one specific point which you've described in your statement, which is a radio conversation which you overheard after the execution had taken place. Do you recall that radio conversation?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Yes, I was just about to speak about that. And as I said, I kind of switched the chronology around. I just wanted to add this in order to avoid any kind of misunderstandings, and then I will answer your question. If you agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Then there was the individual shooting, and, as I said, that I could hear my uncle gurgling. He was shot a second time with a bullet to the head, and that same bullet hit me in the right forearm. And I had the feeling that my arm was blown off. After that, you could hear the radio which I actually noticed before the actual act of the execution took place was in the hands of Paunovic, aka Spiro, and I could hear somebody through it saying, Who is shooting? Then there was an answer by Dragoje Paunovic, aka Spiro: Spiro, Spiro is shooting. And then after that there was a question by Dragoje Paunovic, aka Spiro: Who's asking? And then the answer came: "Rajko Kusic."

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bazdar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's about your request, Mr. Robinson, to postpone the cross-examination of this witness to tomorrow. But having reviewed the changes made by the witness, and in particular given that Mr. Gaynor has kindly went over one by one about those changes, there should be no problem in Mr. Karadzic starting his cross-examination today. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I thought that one more argument for postponement would also be the fact that I cannot finish my cross-examination today, but it's as you decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we have 20 minutes. Let's not waste time. Thank you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Bazdar.

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before I ask any questions, I would like to express my solidarity with you because you survived and because you went through all of those losses. And I would like you to know that during my questioning I do not wish to bring into question anything about you. All I'm seeking to do is to ask you to help us to clarify who was doing what. So I would now like to ask you whether on page 3 of your statement about this 4th or April or the 3rd of June; which one is it?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: It's the 3rd of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then a little bit lower on the same page, the third paragraph down, you said that over the next few days Serb soldiers came house to house and ordered us to move in with families of other Muslims so that they could control us within a smaller number of houses. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: They moved in several families into one house so that it would be easier to monitor those of us who stayed behind. So that it would be easier for them to keep their eye on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And those at were homes of relatives, number of relatives would be placed in one house. Is that right? You said that you were able to go out, you could take care of your cattle, do some little farming work, take care of your household chores, but you didn't go anywhere; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Well, the only thing that we could do is this specifically. In my father's house, there were four or five families, so there was only one family of relatives, actually, and the other families were neighbours. And all we were able to do was go to the stable where the cattle was. That was it. We could take care of the animals so that they wouldn't die. Everything else was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, in other places you said that you could do some small agricultural tasks.

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Well, perhaps it's a question of translation. There were no farms as such. These were just stables with a few animals, and that was it. Perhaps there was some kind of understanding that it was a farm because of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, yeah, it's a question of language. Can you please tell us, in paragraph 6, on page 3, you said that these were Serb soldiers, that they were wearing camouflage uniforms and had SDS insignia. Could you please tell us what SDS insignia is, how does that look like?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: When I say "SDS insignia," I mean the tri-colour insignia, the flag, the red, white, and blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not an SDS insignia. It's a flag.

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. When I was speaking about SDS insignia, I was actually thinking of these characteristic colours, the three colours of the flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And in some places you describe some sort of Chetniks or White Eagles. What were they dressed in and what insignia did they have?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Specifically for the White Eagles they wore camouflage uniforms with red berets on their heads, and they had a two-headed white eagle as a kind of crest on that uniform. And, of course, I could tell by the accent that they were speaking in, in the Ekavica accent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So by their accent you concluded that these were not local Serbs; is that right? Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Yes, when I'm talking about the White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 4 you say that on the 4th of August, 1992, three local Serb soldiers came to your house and said that they were expecting an attack from the Territorial Defence and that they viewed it as a Muslim offensive force. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Yes, three or four. I think there were four of these Serb neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And they said that because of that they were going to take you to the high school facility in Rogatica for your own safety; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Well, actually, it's better to say that they lied to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But that is what they told you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Other than a few men, mostly it was women and children. And do you know that there were a few Serbs in the high school centre as well as a few loyal Muslims who then went home, and these other ones then went to prison? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you say that you were 15 years old at the time; that was one of your corrections. You were always tall, is that right, so that the Serbs thought you were older? This is also something that you said on page 4 in paragraph 5; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't always tall, but when I was 15 I was somewhat taller than my peers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And probably more masculine, more adult; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Well, I've just answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you say on the same page that you had hunting weapons, but then they found 2.000 bullets on you. Was that 2.000 hunting rifle cartridges, or are you talking about bullets? Because 2.000 cartridges takes up a lot of space, does it not?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that I had a hunting rifle. That's not correct. And I did not state that we had 2.000 bullets. What I said was that my father had a hunting weapon for which he had a regular licence or permit. But I was told by the Serbian soldiers, by Kovacevic, I think his name is Radenko, who, on the third day of my captivity, came in an official police vehicle, and he told me that -- i.e., that 2.000 pieces of ammunition were found underneath the bath-tub and that he wanted me to hand over the hunting rifle that belonged to my father.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But then you left and found two hunting rifles that your father had hidden there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you had some sort of work duty and you were doing various kinds of things, cleaning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the Serbs also were subject to work duty? Whoever was not at the front line had to do something according to the All People's Defence law; did you know that?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: No. Since I was 15, I didn't have to know that. And for as long as I was captured, I didn't see any single Serb doing any kind of work that we, captured Muslims, were doing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say on page 5 that a Serb soldier came named Radislav Ljubinac, nicknamed Pjano. Why was that his nickname? Was he well-known as an alcoholic? Because that is a nickname for alcoholics; right?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: I don't know. I just know that this was his name and surname and his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the minibus that they were driving you in, there were two Serbs, a certain Djeric and a certain Nada; right? And you reached Duljevac, that's the name, right?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Yes, Duljevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You saw about 50 Chetniks there. Do you say that all Serbs are Chetniks, like many others do, or was this a separate group that had long hair, beards, characteristic caps? And what was on these caps? You say two-headed eagles, and what about those cross-bones? Can you identify them? Can you describe them? Can you describe what they looked like? What led you to believe that they were Chetniks or to call them that?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: You are putting five questions to me at once. I would like to ask you to put specific questions one by one if you're interested in something in particular. I am not going to give you general answers to general questions like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. How did you ascertain that these were Chetniks, unless you call all Serbs Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: Inter alia, not all of them had those greasy caps of yours, whatever you call them, and cockades with those skulls. There were others wearing camouflage uniforms in addition to these unkept ones, their hygiene was poor, their hair was dirty. There were others, though, with proper haircuts and tidy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 5 you do not mention them. You mention 50 Chetniks. And I'm just asking you: What made you call them Chetniks? Were -- were the two-headed eagles the thing that led you call them Chetniks, or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: ARMIN BAZDAR
utterances.text: I've already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we'll stop here for today. Mr. Gaynor, you would like to address us in the absence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I think that would be best. It's actually Ms. Edgerton who will be making the motion. It will be best in the absence of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bazdar. We'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. So during the course of your evidence, giving testimony, please do not discuss about your evidence with anybody. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, yes, yes. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Please have a pleasant evening. I'll see you tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'm back before you again this afternoon in respect of an oral motion for protective measures that I'd like to make for a subsequent witness, so if we could go into private session for this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, everybody --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? May I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we not do it tomorrow? We're past the time by seven minutes, with the indulgence of the staff.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's just one sentence, though. Actually, I would like to ask you to look at this. Maybe I need to submit a motion in writing, to receive amalgamated statements in Serbian. Neither the witnesses nor I have this in our own language, so it's a major problem. It's late anyway and it's in a foreign language and translations and formulations are sometimes very difficult, they have a double meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
